neurons.title: Hunger
neurons.text: What: When blood sugar drops, patience and self-control fall and anger comes easier ("hangry").

neurons.title: Physical pain
neurons.text: What: Pain narrows attention and lowers patience. Social rejection activates brain regions similar to physical pain: "heartbroken" is not just a metaphor.

neurons.title: Physiological arousal
neurons.text:
What: Increased heart rate, breathing and sweating. The same bodily arousal can be interpreted as fear, anger, excitement or attraction depending on context (two-factor theory). People who survive danger together may be drawn to each other more.
Source: Schachter & Singer; Dutton & Aron, bridge study.

neurons.title: Touch
neurons.text: What: A warm touch releases oxytocin, lowers cortisol and increases trust. The need for touch varies greatly by person and culture; unwanted touch is a threat.

neurons.title: Alcohol
neurons.text: What: Alcohol lowers inhibition: a shy person opens up, an angry person explodes, hidden feelings are spoken. It narrows attention and makes decisions impulsive.

neurons.title: Cognitive biases
neurons.text:
What: Shortcuts (heuristics) the mind uses to decide quickly, and their systematic errors. Humans are not rational calculators; emotions, expectations and identity bend attention, memory and judgment. The "cognitive distortions" of cognitive therapy are the ones linked to emotional problems.
Source: Kahneman & Tversky; Aaron Beck; David Burns.

neurons.title: Confirmation bias
neurons.text: What: Noticing, remembering and inflating information that confirms what one already believes; ignoring what contradicts it. Someone who once decides "this guy can't be trusted" reads every later action through that lens.

neurons.title: First impressions
neurons.text:
What: People judge others within seconds (thin slicing) on warmth and competence; that first judgment becomes an anchor that filters everything after. Changing a first impression is much harder than forming it, especially a negative one.
Source: Ambady & Rosenthal; Fiske, warmth-competence model.

neurons.title: Halo effect
neurons.text: What: One positive trait (especially physical attractiveness) spreading to the whole person: beautiful people are assumed smarter, kinder and more trustworthy. It also works in reverse: one bad trait stains everything.

neurons.title: Negativity bias
neurons.text: What: Bad events are felt and remembered more strongly than good ones. In a relationship it takes about five positive interactions to balance one negative (the Gottman ratio).

neurons.title: Fundamental attribution error
neurons.text: What: Attributing others' behavior to their personality and our own to circumstances. "He was late because he doesn't care; I was late because of traffic."

neurons.title: Self-serving bias
neurons.text: What: Attributing success to oneself and failure to external factors. It protects self-esteem.

neurons.title: In-group bias
neurons.text:
What: Seeing members of one's own group more positively, trusting and favoring them; seeing the out-group as uniform and less human. The group can be something tiny: the same neighborhood, team, universe.
Source: Tajfel, social identity theory.

neurons.title: Prejudice and stereotypes
neurons.text:
What: Applying generalizations about a group (stereotypes) to one member of it and reacting emotionally on that basis (prejudice). It saves mental energy but cannot see the individual. It grows stronger when tired, stressed or threatened. It weakens with real acquaintance, but confirmation bias protects it.
Source: Allport, contact hypothesis.

neurons.title: Hostile attribution bias
neurons.text:
What: Interpreting ambiguous behavior as hostile intent. Thinking someone who bumped your shoulder did it "on purpose". Markedly high in aggressive people, and it triggers anger.
Source: Dodge.

neurons.title: Loss aversion
neurons.text: What: The pain of losing is about twice as strong as the joy of gaining the same amount. People take irrational risks to keep what they have and few risks to gain something new.

neurons.title: Sunk cost
keys: i put so much into this
don't want it to be wasted
neurons.text: What: Staying in a bad relationship or path because of investments (time, effort, emotion) that won't come back.

neurons.title: Cognitive dissonance
neurons.text:
What: The discomfort felt when beliefs and behavior clash. People usually relieve it by changing the belief, not the behavior: valuing what they worked hard for more, trashing the person who left them.
Source: Festinger.

neurons.title: Catastrophizing
neurons.text: What: Treating the worst possible outcome as certain and unbearable. "They didn't reply, there must be someone else, they're going to leave me."

neurons.title: Mind reading
neurons.text: What: Believing you know what another thinks without evidence, usually in a negative direction.

neurons.title: All-or-nothing thinking
neurons.text: What: Unable to see gray areas; something is either total success or total failure, someone is either good or bad.

neurons.title: Personalization
neurons.text: What: Relating events that have nothing to do with oneself to oneself. When the partner comes home tired and quiet, thinking "they're mad at me."

neurons.title: Overgeneralization
neurons.text: What: Drawing a general, permanent rule from a single event. After one breakup: "Nobody will ever love me."

neurons.title: Emotional reasoning
keys: i feel it so it must be
neurons.text: What: Treating feelings as evidence: "I feel jealous, so they must be cheating."

neurons.title: Should statements
neurons.text: What: Rigid rules for oneself and others: "If he loved me, he should have understood." When unmet, anger or guilt follows.

neurons.title: Conflict styles
neurons.text:
What: The Thomas-Kilmann model describes conflict behavior on two dimensions: how much one cares about one's own wishes (assertiveness) and how much about the other's (cooperativeness). Five styles result. Everyone uses all of them but falls back on their dominant style under stress.
Source: Thomas & Kilmann.

neurons.title: Competing style
neurons.text: What: High assertiveness, low cooperation: winning the argument. Decides fast in a crisis, leaves hurt behind in a relationship.

neurons.title: Collaborating style
neurons.text: What: High assertiveness, high cooperation: seeking a solution that meets both sides' needs. Requires time and trust.

neurons.title: Compromising style
neurons.text: What: Moderate assertiveness and cooperation: a quick solution where both give up something.

neurons.title: Avoiding style
neurons.text: What: Low assertiveness, low cooperation: postponing or ignoring the conflict. The problem returns bigger.

neurons.title: Accommodating style
neurons.text: What: Low assertiveness, high cooperation: yielding to the other's wishes. Protects the relationship but anger builds inside.

neurons.title: Dark triad
neurons.text:
What: Three socially aversive traits present in everyone at varying levels: narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy. With sadism they form the "dark tetrad." These traits can look attractive short term (confidence, charisma, boldness) and wear relationships down long term.
Source: Paulhus & Williams.

neurons.title: Narcissism
neurons.text: What: Grandiosity, need for admiration and entitlement. Grandiose narcissism is extraverted and arrogant; vulnerable narcissism is introverted, touchy and envious. It reacts to criticism with anger or cold withdrawal (narcissistic injury). Empathy exists but is used selectively.

neurons.title: Machiavellianism
neurons.text: What: Strategically steering people toward one's goals, cold calculation, bending morality. Patient, plays the long game, knows how to look trustworthy.

neurons.title: Psychopathy
neurons.text: What: Lack of emotional empathy and remorse, fearlessness, impulsiveness, excitement seeking. Dangerous at high levels; at low-moderate levels it can look like composure in a crisis.

neurons.title: Sadism
neurons.text: What: Taking pleasure in another's suffering. Everyday sadism appears in harmless forms too (violent entertainment, enjoying mockery).

neurons.title: Defense mechanisms
neurons.text:
What: Strategies, mostly unconscious, that the mind uses to protect the self from unbearable feelings (anxiety, shame, guilt). Everyone uses them; the difference is their maturity level.
Vaillant's hierarchy: mature (sublimation, humor, anticipation, altruism, suppression), neurotic (displacement, rationalization, intellectualization, reaction formation, repression), immature (projection, passive aggression, acting out, regression), pathological (denial, splitting, dissociation).
As stress rises, people regress to more primitive defenses.
Source: Anna Freud; George Vaillant.

neurons.title: Denial
neurons.text: What: Refusing to accept a painful reality. "We don't have a problem." Someone who doesn't see the signs they're being cheated on.

neurons.title: Splitting
neurons.text: What: Seeing people and oneself as all good or all bad; unable to hold good and bad in the same person. A partner is idealized one day and devalued the next over a single mistake.

neurons.title: Dissociation
neurons.text: What: Disconnecting from emotion, body or reality in an unbearable moment. The person experiences it as if watching and has trouble remembering later.

neurons.title: Projection
neurons.text: What: Attributing one's own unacceptable feelings and urges to someone else. The person thinking about cheating accuses the partner of cheating.

neurons.title: Passive aggression
neurons.text: What: Expressing anger indirectly rather than directly: being late, "forgetting", one-word answers, backhanded compliments, the silent treatment. The person who says "I'm not mad" while every move says they are.

neurons.title: Sarcasm
neurons.text: What: Jabbing with mocking, double-edged remarks. It is both a joke and an attack; because it is deniable, it is a safe way to express anger.

neurons.title: Acting out
neurons.text: What: Discharging an emotion through impulsive action without thinking: slamming doors, flirting with someone else, drinking, breaking things.

neurons.title: Regression
neurons.text: What: Returning to more childlike behavior under stress: whining, sulking, wanting to be taken care of, pouting.

neurons.title: Displacement
keys: why are you mad at me
neurons.text: What: Directing an emotion away from its real source onto a safer target. Someone angry at their boss comes home and yells at their partner.

neurons.title: Rationalization
neurons.text: What: Finding logical-sounding reasons for an emotional or unacceptable behavior. "I didn't want that relationship anyway."

neurons.title: Intellectualization
neurons.text: What: Keeping an emotion at a distance through cold, rational analysis instead of feeling it. Someone describing their breakup like a psychology paper.

neurons.title: Reaction formation
neurons.text: What: Covering an unacceptable feeling by exaggerating its opposite. Someone who likes a person but can't admit it is constantly rude to them.

neurons.title: Repression
neurons.text: What: Keeping a painful memory or urge out of awareness; the person doesn't do it on purpose. That is the difference from conscious suppression.

neurons.title: Sublimation
neurons.text: What: Turning an unacceptable urge or pain into a valued activity: anger into sport, sadness into song, passion into art.

neurons.title: Humor as defense
neurons.text: What: Lightening a painful situation with a joke. A mature defense; but used constantly it blocks intimacy: the person escapes into a joke even in a serious moment.

neurons.title: Anticipation
neurons.text: What: Thinking ahead about a future difficulty and preparing emotionally and practically.

neurons.title: Altruism
neurons.text: What: Easing one's own pain by helping others.

neurons.title: Emotion regulation
neurons.text:
What: The effort to influence which emotion one has, when, how intensely, and how it is expressed. Everyone regulates emotion; the difference is which strategies they use. Healthy strategies (reappraisal, acceptance, seeking support) process the emotion; unhealthy ones (suppression, rumination, avoidance) postpone and magnify it.
Source: Gross, process model.

neurons.title: Emotional expression
neurons.text:
What: Expressing what one feels through face, voice, body and words. Culture, gender roles and family "display rules" teach this: in some families crying is weakness, in others anger is forbidden.
Someone who never shows emotion is not without feeling; the body usually gives it away: a clenched jaw, a thinner voice, eyes that slide away.

neurons.title: Suppression
neurons.text: What: Consciously blocking the outward expression of a felt emotion: saying "I'm fine", smiling it off. It works short term; long term stress rises, memory weakens, and the other person senses something fake, so closeness drops. Suppressed emotion usually explodes somewhere else.

neurons.title: Rumination
neurons.text:
What: Replaying a negative event and feeling over and over; getting stuck on "why?" It produces no solution, prolongs sadness and anger, and feeds depression. Strongest at night, staring at the ceiling.
Source: Nolen-Hoeksema.

neurons.title: Cognitive reappraisal
neurons.text: What: Changing the emotion by reinterpreting the meaning of the event: "He yelled because he was scared, not because he's angry at me." One of the healthiest strategies; it requires flexibility and optimism.

neurons.title: Avoidance
neurons.text: What: Staying away from the person, place, topic or thought that triggers the emotion. It reduces anxiety in the moment but makes fear permanent. In relationships: the "don't bring that up" pattern.

neurons.title: Distraction
neurons.text: What: Moving attention away from the emotion: music, work, phone, sports. Useful in intense moments; as a habit it becomes avoidance.

neurons.title: Acceptance
neurons.text: What: Letting an emotion be felt without trying to change or judge it. Paradox: an accepted emotion passes faster.

neurons.title: Seeking social support
neurons.text: What: Regulating emotion by sharing it with another person. Securely attached people ask for support easily; avoidant people try to handle it alone.

neurons.title: Emotional contagion
neurons.text: What: Other people's emotions passing to us through automatic mimicry of face and voice. We smile next to someone laughing and tense up next to someone tense. It spreads more strongly from people we are close to.

neurons.title: Emotions
neurons.text:
What: An emotion is a bodily, mental and behavioral package about what an event means to the person. The same event creates different emotions in two people, because the appraisal of the event, not the event itself, determines the emotion.
Basic emotions (Ekman, Plutchik): joy, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise. Social emotions (shame, guilt, pride, jealousy) are about who we are in others' eyes.
Emotions feed and transform each other: fear can turn into anger, shame into aggression, sadness into longing.

neurons.title: Appraisal
neurons.text:
What: When something happens, the mind automatically asks: Does this matter to me? Is it good or bad? Who is responsible? Can I cope? Does it fit my values? The answers decide the emotion: important + bad + someone else responsible + I can cope = anger; important + bad + I can't cope = fear; bad + I'm responsible = guilt.
This is why schemas and biases change emotions: the same message creates panic in someone with an abandonment schema and mere curiosity in someone without it.
Source: Lazarus; Scherer, component process model.

neurons.title: Joy
neurons.text: What: Reaching a goal or getting something wanted. The face relaxes, the corners of the eyes crinkle (a genuine Duchenne smile), the voice rises, the body opens and moves. Joy wants to be shared.

neurons.title: Sadness
neurons.text: What: The emotion in the face of loss and what cannot be undone. Energy drops, the body closes, the voice slows, the person withdraws or seeks comfort. Sadness slows and deepens thinking; the person reflects on the past and on meaning.

links.why: sadness for what is far away

neurons.title: Melancholy
neurons.text: What: A chronic, calm, reflective sadness. A melancholic person feels transience even in a beautiful moment and finds a kind of beauty and depth in sorrow. Unlike clinical depression, functioning continues and creativity may even increase.

neurons.title: Hopelessness
neurons.text:
What: Believing the future won't be better. Motivation collapses; the person stops trying. The emotional face of learned helplessness.
Source: Seligman, learned helplessness.

neurons.title: Anger
neurons.text:
What: The emotion that directs energy toward resisting an obstacle, injustice or attack. Brows lower, the jaw tightens, the voice rises, the heart speeds up, the body leans forward. Anger says "this is wrong and must be fixed."
Under anger there is often another emotion: hurt, fear, shame. Anger is the shield that covers them.
Women and men feel anger equally often; the way it is expressed and how society reacts differ.

neurons.title: Fear
neurons.text: What: The survival response to threat. Eyes widen, breathing quickens, muscles tense; the body prepares to flee, fight or freeze. Fear belongs to concrete present danger, anxiety to vague future danger.

neurons.title: Anxiety
neurons.text: What: Constant vigilance about a vague, future threat. The anxious mind produces "what if...?" scenarios and tries to control and seek reassurance. Anxiety causes palpitations, a knotted stomach and sleeplessness.

neurons.title: Disgust
neurons.text: What: A protective emotion against contamination; it extends from spoiled food to moral filth. The nose wrinkles, the lip rises, the body pulls back. Moral disgust (betrayal, hypocrisy) produces some of the strongest judgments.

neurons.title: Surprise
neurons.text: What: A brief halt in the face of the unexpected. Brows rise, the mouth opens. Surprise quickly turns into another emotion: joy or fear.

neurons.title: Shame
neurons.text:
What: The feeling "I am bad, I am flawed"; the gaze turns onto the whole self. The face flushes, the eyes drop, the body shrinks, the person wants to hide. Unlike guilt: guilt says "I did a bad thing", shame says "I am a bad person."
Because shame is so painful it is often converted into anger (the shame-rage spiral).
Source: Tangney; Brené Brown.

neurons.title: Guilt
neurons.text: What: The feeling "I did something bad." It focuses on behavior and pushes toward repair: apologies, making amends. Healthy guilt protects relationships; excessive, chronic guilt pushes a person to punish themselves.

neurons.title: Regret
neurons.text: What: Wishing something done or left undone had gone differently. In the long run people regret what they didn't do more than what they did.

neurons.title: Pride
neurons.text: What: The feeling that rises at one's own achievement or worth. The body straightens, the chest opens. Healthy pride rests on achievement; arrogant pride rests on superiority.

neurons.title: Hurt
neurons.text: What: Feeling devalued by someone who matters. A mix of anger and sadness. A hurt person goes quiet, keeps distance or jabs; often waits for an apology without asking for one.

neurons.title: Jealousy
neurons.text:
What: Fear of losing a valued relationship to a rival. A mix of fear, anger and shame. A jealous person watches, questions, compares, belittles the rival or punishes the partner.
It evolved to protect relationships; out of proportion it destroys them.

neurons.title: Envy
neurons.text: What: Wanting what someone else has and resenting them for having it. Jealousy involves three people (fear of losing), envy two (pain of not having).

neurons.title: Longing
neurons.text: What: A bittersweet pull toward a person, place or time that is far away or lost. Longing hurts and also keeps the bond alive.

neurons.title: Nostalgia
neurons.text: What: A sweet-sad longing for the past. Nostalgia reduces loneliness and gives a sense of meaning and continuity; people retreat into it in hard times.

neurons.title: Loneliness
neurons.text:
What: The pain of the gap between wanted and existing relationships. It can be felt in a crowd. Long loneliness makes the brain more alert to threat: the lonely person expects rejection more and becomes more suspicious, which isolates them further.
Source: Cacioppo.

neurons.title: Disappointment
neurons.text: What: The emotion of the drop between expectation and reality. The more idealized, the harder the fall.

neurons.title: Compassion
neurons.text: What: Seeing another's suffering and wanting to ease it. The voice softens, the body approaches, the urge to touch arises.

neurons.title: Gratitude
neurons.text: What: Noticing someone's unearned kindness. It strengthens the relationship and creates the urge to give back.

neurons.title: Relief
neurons.text: What: The expected bad thing not happening or passing. The body relaxes, a deep breath, sometimes tears or laughter.

neurons.title: Awe
neurons.text: What: A feeling of shrinking and expanding before something vast and extraordinary. It makes the self small and increases connection.

neurons.title: Boredom
neurons.text: What: Lack of meaning and stimulation. For an excitement seeker boredom is painful and pushes toward risky behavior.

neurons.title: Contempt
neurons.text: What: Seeing the other as beneath oneself; a one-sided lift of the lip. The most toxic emotion in relationships; according to Gottman, the strongest predictor of divorce.

neurons.title: Mood
neurons.text: What: An emotional background without a specific object, lasting hours or days. Mood colors interpretation: in a bad mood a neutral remark sounds like criticism. Sleep, hunger, weather, hormones and small events affect mood.

neurons.title: Mood swings
neurons.text: What: Mood shifting within a short time from small triggers. Increases with neuroticism and stress.

neurons.title: Humor styles
neurons.text:
What: Humor has four styles: affiliative (making others laugh to bond), self-enhancing (being able to laugh in hardship), aggressive (mockery, put-downs, jabs), self-defeating (getting laughs by putting oneself down). The first two are healthy, the last two have a cost. Humor is also a signal of flirting and intelligence.
Source: Rod Martin.

neurons.title: Affiliative humor
neurons.text: What: Strengthening relationships and easing tension by making others laugh.

neurons.title: Self-enhancing humor
neurons.text: What: Seeing the comic side of hard situations; coping with stress.

neurons.title: Aggressive humor
neurons.text: What: Getting laughs by ridiculing and jabbing others. It establishes superiority and carries anger.

neurons.title: Self-defeating humor
neurons.text: What: Getting laughs by putting oneself down; to win approval or hide pain.

neurons.title: Memory
neurons.text: What: Memory is not a recording device but a story rebuilt with every recall. What gets remembered is decided by what an event meant to the person: emotional intensity, personal significance, repetition and reminding cues. Unimportant things fade fast; meaningful and emotional ones last for years, though details may drift.

neurons.title: Working memory
neurons.text: What: The small space of information held in mind right now (about four items). Stress, fatigue and strong emotion shrink it: an angry person can't think complexly.

neurons.title: Episodic memory
neurons.text: What: Memory of specific lived events: what happened, where, with whom, what I felt. The material of personal identity.

neurons.title: Semantic memory
neurons.text: What: General knowledge independent of events: "She takes her coffee without sugar." Episodic memories turn into semantic knowledge over time; the event is forgotten, the lesson remains.

neurons.title: Emotional memory
neurons.text:
What: Emotionally intense events (joy, fear, shame, love) are encoded much more strongly via the amygdala. Even ordinary details around an important moment (what they wore, the smell of the air) can last for years. A small gesture from someone one cares about can outlast a big statement from someone one doesn't.
Source: McGaugh; flashbulb memory research.

neurons.title: Forgetting curve
neurons.text:
What: Most new information is forgotten quickly in the first days, then the decline slows. The rate of forgetting drops with importance, emotion and repetition. Forgotten things are usually not erased, just inaccessible; the right cue can bring them back.
Source: Ebbinghaus.

neurons.title: Consolidation
neurons.text: What: The more often a memory is recalled, discussed and thought about, the stronger it becomes. Sleep consolidates the day's memories.

neurons.title: Reconsolidation
neurons.text: What: With every recall a memory is rewritten and shifts with present feelings and beliefs. A couple who broke up remember the past as worse; a couple who reunited remember it as better. Two people remember the same event differently.

neurons.title: Prospective memory
neurons.text: What: Remembering to do something in the future: dates, promises, birthdays. Intentions that matter and carry emotion are remembered; ones seen as unimportant slip easily. "I forgot" often means "it didn't matter to me", and the other person reads it that way.

neurons.title: Cue-dependent recall
neurons.text: What: A smell, song, place or word can suddenly revive the memory tied to it. Things thought forgotten return with the right cue.

neurons.title: Motivated forgetting
keys: don't want to think about it
neurons.text: What: Constant avoidance of painful memories weakening them.

neurons.title: Needs
neurons.text:
What: The engines beneath behavior. Self-Determination Theory names three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness. When they are met people thrive; when blocked, anger, anxiety, defensiveness and compensating behaviors appear. Maslow's ordering isn't rigid, but when physiological and safety needs are threatened, people push closeness and meaning aside.
Source: Deci & Ryan; Maslow; Baumeister & Leary.

neurons.title: Autonomy
neurons.text: What: The need to own one's behavior and make one's own choices. When blocked, the person resists, digs in, does the opposite (psychological reactance). A controlling partner sparks rebellion in someone with high autonomy needs.

neurons.title: Psychological reactance
neurons.text:
What: When freedom is threatened, wanting the forbidden thing more and doing the opposite. What is forbidden becomes more attractive.
Source: Brehm.

neurons.title: Stubbornness
neurons.text: What: Not leaving a position despite evidence and cost. It often protects autonomy and pride; backing down feels like defeat.

neurons.title: Need for competence
neurons.text: What: The need to feel effective and capable. When blocked, a person gives up or tries to prove themselves in another area.

neurons.title: Need to belong
neurons.text: What: The need to be valued, loved, and connected to a group and relationships. As basic as food and sleep; exclusion activates brain regions similar to physical pain.

neurons.title: Need for safety
neurons.text: What: The need to be physically and emotionally safe in a predictable world. If unmet in childhood, it continues in adulthood as constant vigilance, control and mistrust.

neurons.title: Need for control
neurons.text: What: The need to predict and steer events, people and the future. It reduces anxiety. Excessive, it becomes managing and interrogating a partner and tensing at anything unplanned.

neurons.title: Need for admiration
neurons.text: What: The need to be seen, appreciated and considered special. Everyone has it; in narcissism it becomes insatiable. When not appreciated, a person gets hurt or seeks attention elsewhere.

neurons.title: Search for meaning
neurons.text:
What: Feeling that life is tied to a purpose, a story, a value. It comes forward in loss and crisis; suffering that has meaning becomes bearable.
Source: Frankl.

neurons.title: Need for stimulation
neurons.text: What: Every brain has an optimal arousal level. Below it, it gets bored and seeks stimulation; above it, it gets overwhelmed and withdraws. This threshold shapes extraversion and excitement seeking.

neurons.title: Approach and avoidance
neurons.text:
What: Two basic motivational systems: approaching reward (behavioral activation) and avoiding threat (behavioral inhibition). One moves in a relationship to "win", the other to "not lose". Avoidance-focused people don't take risks and miss chances; approach-focused people jump in and sometimes get burned.
Source: Gray, reinforcement sensitivity theory.

neurons.title: Procrastination
neurons.text: What: Delaying what must be done while knowing the cost. Not laziness but emotional avoidance: escaping the discomfort, anxiety or fear of failure the task creates.

neurons.title: Instant gratification
neurons.text: What: Wanting pleasure here and now; trading long-term gain for short-term pleasure. Inability to wait for a delayed reward (the marshmallow test).

neurons.title: Risk taking
neurons.text: What: Acting for reward despite possible loss. It rises with excitement seeking and impulsiveness and falls with anxiety. Romantic and sexual risk is included.

neurons.title: Personality
neurons.text:
What: A person's relatively stable pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving across time and situations. The strongest scientific model is the Big Five: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness. Personality is shaped by genes (roughly 40-50% heritable) and experience, and becomes more stable after the early thirties.
Important: Personality does not determine behavior, it shifts its probability. The same person can act differently in different contexts (person x situation interaction).
Source: McCrae & Costa, Five-Factor Model; HEXACO (Ashton & Lee).

links.why: how a person narrates their own personality

neurons.title: Temperament
neurons.text:
What: Inborn tendencies of reactivity visible even in infancy: how quickly one is aroused, how intensely one reacts, how fast one calms down. The biological base of personality.
Example: Some babies shrink away from strangers (behavioral inhibition), others crawl toward them. This tendency persists into adulthood as shyness or sociability.
Source: Kagan; Thomas & Chess.

links.why: adult form of an inhibited temperament

neurons.title: Extraversion
neurons.text:
What: The direction of energy. Extraverts gain energy from social stimulation, feel positive emotions more often and more intensely, and are more sensitive to reward. Introverts recharge alone; they are not socially unskilled, they simply saturate on stimulation faster.
Facets: warmth, gregariousness, assertiveness, energy, excitement seeking, positive emotionality.
In conversation: Extraverts talk fast and a lot, open topics, fill silences. Introverts speak thoughtfully and briefly and prefer deep conversations to small talk.

neurons.title: Warmth
neurons.text:
What: The tendency to show genuine interest and affection toward others. Warm people become close quickly, smile, touch, use names. Cold people can be polite but keep emotional distance.
Note: Coldness is not always a lack of love; it is often a protective strategy.

neurons.title: Gregariousness
neurons.text: What: Preferring to be with people. High gregariousness seeks crowds and finds solitude boring; low gregariousness prefers few but deep relationships.

neurons.title: Assertiveness
neurons.text: What: The tendency to speak up, lead and say what one wants plainly. An assertive person makes the first move, starts the flirt, runs the meeting.

neurons.title: Energy and enthusiasm
neurons.text: What: The tempo of life. High-energy people talk fast, walk fast, do many things at once. Low-energy people are calm and slow-paced.

neurons.title: Positive emotionality
neurons.text: What: The tendency to experience positive emotions like joy, delight and amusement often. The strongest marker of extraversion.

neurons.title: Excitement seeking
neurons.text:
What: The need for new, intense, risky stimulation. High excitement seekers cannot stand boredom and want speed, danger, new partners, new experiences.
Source: Zuckerman, sensation seeking.

neurons.title: Agreeableness
neurons.text:
What: The tendency to maintain social harmony. Agreeable people trust, help, compromise and consider others' feelings. Low agreeableness is competitive, skeptical, blunt and tough.
Women score slightly higher on average, but individual differences are far larger than the gender difference.
Facets: trust, straightforwardness, altruism, compliance, modesty, tender-mindedness.

neurons.title: Compliance
neurons.text: What: The tendency to back down in conflict, hold anger in and meet the other halfway. Low compliance wants to win the argument, takes offense easily and wants the last word.

neurons.title: Conscientiousness
neurons.text:
What: The tendency to control impulses, plan and stick to goals. High conscientiousness: organized, reliable, keeps promises, careful. Low: spontaneous, flexible, messy, lives in the moment; may forget dates and promises.
Facets: sense of competence, order, dutifulness, achievement striving, self-discipline, deliberation.

neurons.title: Orderliness
neurons.text: What: The need to keep one's space and time in order. High orderliness is bothered by mess; low orderliness is comfortable in chaos.

neurons.title: Dutifulness
neurons.text: What: Keeping one's word and honoring rules and obligations. A highly dutiful person feels heavy guilt when breaking a promise.

neurons.title: Self-discipline
neurons.text: What: Keeping at a boring or hard task until it is done. Low self-discipline postpones and leaves things half-finished.

neurons.title: Deliberation
neurons.text: What: Thinking before acting. Low deliberation says whatever comes to mind and decides without thinking.

neurons.title: Sense of competence
neurons.text: What: Feeling skilled and effective. When it is low, a person starts with "I can't."

neurons.title: Neuroticism
neurons.text:
What: The tendency to experience negative emotions (anxiety, anger, sadness, shame) often and intensely, and vulnerability to stress. High neuroticism sees threats faster, treats uncertainty as danger, takes criticism personally and replays events for a long time.
Facets: anxiety, angry hostility, depression, self-consciousness, impulsiveness, vulnerability.
In the brain: a more reactive amygdala; faster and longer reactions to threat.

neurons.title: Vulnerability
neurons.text: What: Falling apart under stress and pressure, getting hurt easily. A vulnerable person freezes or collapses in hard moments and is affected by criticism for days.

neurons.title: Impulsiveness
neurons.text: What: Acting immediately on urges and feelings; being unable to delay. An impulsive person sends the angry text and regrets it; shops, kisses, fights when the urge hits.

neurons.title: Openness to experience
neurons.text:
What: Openness to new ideas, experiences, feelings and aesthetics. High openness has a rich imagination, is sensitive to art, drawn to the unusual, morally and politically flexible. Low openness likes the concrete, familiar and traditional.
Facets: imagination, aesthetic sensitivity, openness to feelings, novelty seeking, curiosity, openness to values.

neurons.title: Imagination
neurons.text: What: Building vivid scenarios, stories and alternative worlds in the mind. A dreamer lives a future date many times in their head.

neurons.title: Aesthetic sensitivity
neurons.text: What: Being deeply moved by beauty, art, music and nature. A song or a view gives them goosebumps.

neurons.title: Curiosity
neurons.text: What: Intellectual hunger for ideas, people and the unknown. A curious person asks questions, wants to learn the other's story and is drawn to uncertainty rather than afraid of it.

neurons.title: Novelty seeking
neurons.text: What: Getting bored of routine and wanting to try new places, foods and activities.

neurons.title: Openness to values
neurons.text: What: Readiness to question authority, tradition and norms. When high, the person does not shy away from breaking taboos.

neurons.title: Relationships
neurons.text: What: A bond in which two people mutually affect each other's lives. Romantic relationships begin with attraction, deepen through intimacy and trust, and last through commitment; how conflict and repair are handled decides how long they live.

neurons.title: Attraction
neurons.text: What: The pull toward someone. Known drivers: physical attractiveness, proximity and repeated contact (mere exposure), similarity (in values and attitudes), reciprocal liking (we're drawn to those who like us), a balance of availability (some uncertainty and mystery increases attraction), arousal (the bridge study: fear and adrenaline can be read as attraction).

neurons.title: Physical attractiveness
neurons.text: What: The strongest factor in first impressions. Symmetry, signs of health and cultural beauty norms play a role. But as people get to know each other, personality changes attractiveness: loved people look more beautiful over time.

neurons.title: Similarity effect
neurons.text: What: We're more drawn to people with similar values, attitudes, humor and backgrounds; similarity feels like validation. "Opposites attract" is rarely true for personality, though complementarity (one dominant, one agreeable) sometimes works.

neurons.title: Mere exposure effect
neurons.text: What: The more often we see something, the more we like it. Neighbors, coworkers, people who meet at the same café every day.

neurons.title: Mystery and uncertainty
neurons.text: What: Not being sure whether someone likes us makes us think about them more and raises attraction. Too much creates anxiety and turns repellent.

neurons.title: Flirting
neurons.text:
What: A game of showing interest deniably: long looks, smiles, teasing, light touches, compliments, innuendo. Uncertainty is the engine of flirting; once interest is said plainly, the game ends and the relationship begins.
Styles: playful, sincere, physical, polite (traditional), shy.
Source: Hall, flirting styles.

neurons.title: Playfulness
neurons.text: What: Adult play: teasing, ribbing, role-play, being silly. Playful couples are happier; play is a sign of trust.

neurons.title: Self-disclosure
neurons.text:
What: Sharing personal information, feelings and secrets. Intimacy forms through mutual, gradual disclosure: one opens up, the other responds with understanding and opens up too. Opening up too fast scares; never opening up creates distance. The 36 questions study brought two strangers close in 45 minutes.
Source: Altman & Taylor, social penetration theory; Aron.

neurons.title: Intimacy building
neurons.text:
What: Feeling that someone sees, understands and cares about us. Intimacy forms when self-disclosure meets a responsive answer (interpersonal process model of intimacy).
Source: Reis & Shaver.

neurons.title: Triangle of love
neurons.text: What: Sternberg's three components of love: intimacy (emotional bond), passion (physical and romantic attraction), commitment (the decision to stay together). All three is consummate love; passion alone is infatuation; intimacy plus commitment is companionate love.

neurons.title: Passion
neurons.text: What: Intense physical and emotional longing. Highest at the start of a relationship and tends to fade; novelty, adventure and separation rekindle it.

neurons.title: Commitment
neurons.text: What: The decision to maintain the relationship. Strengthened by satisfaction, lack of alternatives and investments made (Rusbult).

neurons.title: Romantic love
neurons.text:
What: A state running on the brain's dopamine reward system, similar to addiction: constantly thinking of the loved one, finding everything about them meaningful, withdrawal during separation. Idealization is strong early on; within one or two years intensity drops and turns into attachment.
Source: Helen Fisher.

neurons.title: Romantic idealism
neurons.text: What: Believing true love is a single, fated, perfect bond. It feeds romantic imagination but is vulnerable to disappointment in real relationships.

neurons.title: Love styles
neurons.text: What: John Lee's ways of loving: Eros (passionate), Ludus (game), Storge (friendship), Pragma (practical), Mania (obsessive), Agape (selfless). Everyone carries a mix; linked to attachment style (anxious people lean toward Mania, avoidant toward Ludus).

neurons.title: Eros
neurons.text: What: Passionate love that starts with physical attraction and an intense emotional bond. Starts fast, burns hot.

neurons.title: Ludus
neurons.text: What: Love as a game; fun, flirting, relationships with many people without attachment.

neurons.title: Storge
neurons.text: What: Calm, trust-based love that grows slowly out of friendship.

neurons.title: Pragma
neurons.text: What: Choosing a compatible, sensible partner who fits one's life plan.

neurons.title: Mania
neurons.text: What: Obsessive, jealous, up-and-down love; a constant need to confirm being loved.

neurons.title: Agape
neurons.text: What: Selfless, unconditional love that expects nothing back.

neurons.title: Love languages
neurons.text: What: Gary Chapman's popular model: people express and receive love in different ways. Scientific support is limited, but it explains a difference: one expects love in words, another through touch; when languages don't match, "they don't love me" arises.

neurons.title: Words of affirmation
neurons.text: What: Showing and receiving love through words and compliments.

neurons.title: Quality time
neurons.text: What: Spending time together with undivided attention.

neurons.title: Gifts
neurons.text: What: Concrete proof of having been thought of. Its value lies in meaning, not price: "They thought of me."

neurons.title: Acts of service
neurons.text: What: Showing love by doing: cooking, handling their errands.

neurons.title: Physical touch
neurons.text: What: Showing and receiving love through touch.

neurons.title: Relationship stages
neurons.text: What: Knapp's model: initiating, experimenting, intensifying, integrating, bonding; and in coming apart: differentiating, circumscribing, stagnating, avoiding, terminating. Talk changes at each stage: small talk at first, then "we" language.

neurons.title: Building trust
neurons.text:
What: Trust is built in small "sliding door" moments: when one needs the other, does the other turn toward them? Consistency, keeping one's word, responding to vulnerability.
Source: Gottman, trust metric.

neurons.title: Gottman's four horsemen
neurons.text:
What: The four communication patterns that most strongly predict the end of a relationship: criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling.
Source: John Gottman.

neurons.title: Criticism
keys: what kind of person are you
neurons.text: What: Attacking the person rather than the behavior: "You're always selfish." The difference from a complaint: "You didn't call yesterday, I was hurt."

neurons.title: Defensiveness
neurons.text: What: Defending oneself or counterattacking instead of taking responsibility for a criticism.

neurons.title: Stonewalling
neurons.text: What: Shutting down and not responding in an argument; often the "shutdown" response of an overaroused body.

neurons.title: Repair attempts
neurons.text: What: Small moves that stop an argument from escalating: a joke, a touch, an apology, saying "you're right." Happy couples don't avoid fights; they accept repair attempts.

neurons.title: Jealousy and rivalry
neurons.text: What: The threat a third person (real or imagined) creates in a relationship. Men react slightly more to sexual infidelity and women to emotional infidelity; the difference is small and debated.

neurons.title: Possessiveness
neurons.text: What: Seeing the loved one as one's own; claiming their time, attention and body. In moderation it feels like belonging; in excess it is control and suffocation.

neurons.title: Forgiveness
neurons.text: What: The decision and process of letting go of revenge and hurt after being wronged. Forgiving is not forgetting or reconciling. A sincere apology, empathy and the value of the relationship make it easier.

neurons.title: Grudge
neurons.text: What: The chronic anger of an injustice kept alive. Fed by rumination; permanently colors attitude and memory toward the person.

neurons.title: Revenge
neurons.text: What: The urge and act of making someone pay for harm done. Brings brief satisfaction and usually prolongs rumination.

neurons.title: Breakup and loss
neurons.text: What: Losing someone one is attached to. Grief stages aren't linear: denial, anger, bargaining, sadness and acceptance overlap. In a romantic breakup the brain goes through withdrawal; the one who is left wants the other more for a while (frustration attraction).

neurons.title: Schemas
neurons.text:
What: Deep, lasting belief-feeling patterns about self, others and the world, formed when core needs went unmet in childhood. When a schema is triggered, the person reacts to the old wound, not the present event: the reaction is out of proportion.
People cope with schemas in three ways: surrender (choosing relationships that confirm the schema), avoidance (staying away from triggering situations), overcompensation (doing the opposite; someone who feels defective acting arrogant).
Young describes 18 schemas in five domains: disconnection and rejection, impaired autonomy, impaired limits, other-directedness, overvigilance.
Source: Jeffrey Young, Schema Therapy.

neurons.title: Abandonment schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "The people I love will eventually leave or are unreliable."
Origin: Loss of a parent, divorce, inconsistent attention, frequent moves.
When triggered: A small distance feels like catastrophe; clinging, jealousy, or leaving first.

neurons.title: Mistrust schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "People will hurt me, deceive me, use me."
Origin: Abuse, being cheated on, humiliation.
When triggered: Suspicion, testing, attacking first, guarding secrets.

neurons.title: Emotional deprivation schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "My emotional needs will never be met; no one will truly understand me."
Origin: Cold, inattentive care.
When triggered: Never stating needs, or deep anger when they go unmet.

neurons.title: Defectiveness schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I am fundamentally flawed; if people really knew me they wouldn't love me."
Origin: Criticism, humiliation, rejection.
When triggered: Shame, hiding oneself, suspicion of compliments; arrogance in overcompensation.

neurons.title: Social isolation schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I'm different; I don't belong to any group."
When triggered: Standing at the edges of groups, alienation.

neurons.title: Dependence schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I can't handle everyday life without others' help."
When triggered: Indecision, constantly asking advice, fear of being alone.

neurons.title: Vulnerability to harm schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "Catastrophe can strike at any moment and I can't prevent it."
When triggered: Excessive precaution, anxiety, catastrophizing.

neurons.title: Enmeshment schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I'm not a full person without someone else (often a parent)."
When triggered: Unable to draw boundaries, dissolving identity into the relationship.

neurons.title: Failure schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I have failed and will fail; I'm not as talented as my peers."
When triggered: Not trying, procrastinating, self-sabotage.

neurons.title: Entitlement schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I'm special; rules are for other people."
When triggered: Demandingness, lack of empathy, ignoring limits.

neurons.title: Insufficient self-control schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I can't tolerate discomfort and frustration."
When triggered: Impulsiveness, quitting halfway, instant gratification.

neurons.title: Subjugation schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "If I say what I want they'll get angry or leave; I must submit."
When triggered: Can't say no, storing anger inside, passive aggression.

neurons.title: Self-sacrifice schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "Others' needs come before mine."
When triggered: Wearing oneself out, then feeling hurt at not being noticed.

neurons.title: Approval-seeking schema
keys: what do you think of me
neurons.text:
Belief: "My worth depends on others' approval."
When triggered: Adjusting behavior to be liked, hypersensitivity to criticism.

neurons.title: Negativity schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "Things eventually go wrong."
When triggered: Magnifying the negative, minimizing the positive, not allowing joy.

neurons.title: Emotional inhibition schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "Showing my feelings is dangerous or shameful."
When triggered: Coldness, overcontrol, appearing emotionless.

neurons.title: Unrelenting standards schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "I must meet very high standards or I'm worthless."
When triggered: Perfectionism, rigidity, inability to enjoy.

neurons.title: Punitiveness schema
neurons.text:
Belief: "Whoever makes mistakes, including me, should be punished."
When triggered: Inability to forgive, harshness toward self and others.

neurons.title: Self-concept
neurons.text:
What: The set of beliefs a person holds about themselves: who they are, what they're good at, what kind of person they are. People want to see themselves consistently and seek feedback that confirms their self-concept; someone who sees themselves as worthless may distrust even a partner who treats them well (self-verification).
Source: Swann, self-verification theory; Rogers.

neurons.title: Self-esteem
neurons.text:
What: The overall value a person gives themselves. According to sociometer theory, self-esteem is a gauge of acceptance; it drops with rejection. Low self-esteem expects rejection and receives compliments with suspicion. Fragile high self-esteem (in narcissism) looks strong outside but is extremely sensitive to criticism.
Source: Leary, sociometer theory.

neurons.title: Rejection sensitivity
neurons.text:
What: Anxiously expecting rejection, perceiving ambiguous signals as rejection, and reacting intensely (anger or withdrawal). It becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Source: Downey & Feldman.

neurons.title: Identity
neurons.text:
What: The story a person tells about themselves: origin, roles, values, groups they belong to, and a narrative stretching from past to future. Narrative identity lets a person make sense of pain: "It made me stronger."
Source: McAdams.

neurons.title: Body image
neurons.text: What: A person's perception of and feelings about their body. Negative body image creates shame and avoidance in intimacy.

neurons.title: Perfectionism
neurons.text: What: Very high standards and intolerance of mistakes. Its adaptive form brings achievement; its maladaptive form brings fear of failure, procrastination and endless self-criticism.

neurons.title: Impostor syndrome
neurons.text: What: Feeling that one doesn't deserve one's success and will one day be "found out", despite being successful.

neurons.title: Self-compassion
neurons.text:
What: Treating oneself in hard moments the way one would treat a friend. Accepting a mistake without denying it or tearing oneself apart. A sturdier base than self-esteem.
Source: Kristin Neff.

neurons.title: Arrogance
neurons.text: What: Seeing oneself as above others and showing it. Often the armor of fragile self-esteem.

neurons.title: Humility
neurons.text: What: Not presenting oneself as bigger than one is, sharing credit, accepting one's limits. In excess: inability to accept praise and putting oneself down.

neurons.title: Optimism
neurons.text:
What: Positive expectation about the future. Optimists explain bad events as temporary, specific and external; pessimists as permanent, pervasive and personal (explanatory style).
Source: Seligman.

neurons.title: Sexuality
neurons.text: What: The domain of sexual desire, arousal, intimacy and identity. Personality, attachment style, values, shame and past experiences shape sexuality deeply. Anxiously attached people tend to use sex for reassurance and closeness; avoidant people experience it while keeping distance.

neurons.title: Sexual desire
neurons.text:
What: The wish for sexual intimacy. It can be spontaneous (appearing suddenly) or responsive (emerging slowly through closeness and stimulation); in many people, especially in long relationships, responsive desire dominates. Stress, fatigue and anger shut desire down; novelty, play and a hint of danger raise it.
Source: Basson; Nagoski, dual control model (accelerator and brakes).

neurons.title: Sociosexuality
neurons.text:
What: How independent sexuality is from emotional bonding and commitment. Restricted people need a bond and time; unrestricted people can keep sex separate from attachment.
Source: Simpson & Gangestad.

neurons.title: Consent
neurons.text: What: Mutual, willing and revocable-at-any-moment agreement in every intimate step. No is always no; hesitation is also a signal. Consent is the most concrete form of respecting boundaries.

neurons.title: Fantasy
neurons.text: What: Desire staged in the mind. Fantasies reveal a person's wishes, fears and hidden needs (control, surrender, being desired).

neurons.title: Social cognition
neurons.text: What: The mental processes humans use to understand, judge, predict and relate to others. We are a social species: a large part of the brain is devoted to "what is he thinking, what will she do to me, what am I in their eyes."

neurons.title: Theory of mind
neurons.text: What: Understanding that others have their own beliefs, desires and intentions, and predicting them. The ability that answers "is she joking or serious?" Reading hints, sarcasm and flirting depends on it.

neurons.title: Intelligence and inference
neurons.text: What: Processing information quickly, making connections, thinking abstractly and drawing conclusions. Social intelligence and academic intelligence differ; one reads hints, the other solves problems. Intelligent people bore more easily and love wordplay and irony.

neurons.title: Empathy
neurons.text: What: Two kinds: cognitive empathy (understanding what someone feels) and emotional empathy (feeling it with them). In psychopathy cognitive empathy can be intact while emotional empathy is weak; that is what makes manipulation possible. Empathy is stronger toward close, similar and loved people.

neurons.title: Trust
neurons.text:
What: The expectation that the other will not hurt us and will keep their word. It is built through small steps, consistency and positive responses to vulnerability; a single betrayal collapses it. General trustfulness is part of personality; trust in a specific person is formed through experience.
Three components: competence (can they), benevolence (will they treat me well), integrity (do they tell the truth).

neurons.title: Betrayal of trust
neurons.text: What: A trusted person violating expectations. Betrayal doesn't just hurt; it rewrites the past: "So he was lying back then too." Repair takes long, consistent effort.

neurons.title: Skepticism
neurons.text: What: Not believing words and intentions without evidence. Healthy skepticism protects; too much makes intimacy impossible.

neurons.title: Reciprocity
neurons.text: What: The norm of returning good for good and bad for bad; present in every culture. When someone opens up, we open up; whoever receives a gift feels obliged to give back.

neurons.title: Social comparison
neurons.text:
What: Evaluating oneself by comparing with others. Upward comparison (with someone better) can motivate but creates envy and low self-esteem; downward comparison comforts.
Source: Festinger.

neurons.title: Power and status
neurons.text: What: Who makes the decisions in a relationship, who needs whom more. The principle of least interest: "whoever cares less holds more power." Loss of status (humiliation, ridicule) is one of the strongest triggers of anger.

neurons.title: Dominance
neurons.text: What: The tendency to steer, decide and set the limits in a setting or relationship. Its healthy form is leadership; its excess is control and domination. Some people prefer the dominant role in relationships, others the yielding one; this preference can also show in sexuality.

neurons.title: Conformity
neurons.text: What: The tendency to follow group norms and expectations. In Asch's experiments a third of people went along with an obvious error because the group did.

neurons.title: Impression management
neurons.text: What: Adjusting behavior to create a desired image in others' eyes. Everyone plays a role on stage (Goffman); close relationships are like backstage, where the role drops.

neurons.title: Boundaries
neurons.text: What: Deciding and protecting what one allows and doesn't. Healthy boundaries allow both closeness and independence. Someone who can't set boundaries stores anger inside.

neurons.title: Shyness
neurons.text: What: Holding back in front of new and important people out of fear of social evaluation. A shy person feels anxiety, not disinterest; their silence can be mistaken for coldness.

neurons.title: Social anxiety
neurons.text: What: Intense fear of others' negative evaluation; avoiding speaking and drawing attention.

neurons.title: Honesty
neurons.text: What: Not deceiving others, acting fairly, not manipulating for one's own gain (HEXACO honesty-humility). High honesty can't even tell a white lie; low honesty bends the truth as convenient.

neurons.title: Lying
neurons.text: What: People tell one or two lies a day on average; most are white lies that grease social life. Lying raises cognitive load: hesitation, too much detail or the opposite, too little. A caught lie destroys trust.

neurons.title: Manipulation
neurons.text: What: Steering the other secretly rather than openly: guilt-tripping, gaslighting (making them doubt reality), using love as reward and punishment, making them jealous, the silent treatment.

neurons.title: Stress
neurons.text:
What: The perception that demands exceed one's resources to cope. The body prepares for threat with cortisol and adrenaline; attention narrows, thinking becomes rigid, patience drops, and people fall back on primitive defenses and automatic reactions. Short stress sharpens, chronic stress depletes.
Four reflexes in the face of threat: fight, flight, freeze, fawn.
Source: Selye; Lazarus & Folkman; Walker (the four Fs).

neurons.title: Fight response
neurons.text: What: Resisting threat by attacking: raising the voice, trying to win the argument, physical aggression.

neurons.title: Aggression
neurons.text:
What: Behavior intended to harm another. Two kinds: reactive (angry, hot, sudden) and instrumental (cold, for a goal). It appears as verbal aggression (insults, humiliation), relational aggression (gossip, exclusion) and physical aggression.
Source: Anderson & Bushman, general aggression model.

neurons.title: Flight response
neurons.text: What: Moving away from the threat: leaving the room, ending the relationship, burying oneself in work, changing the subject.

neurons.title: Freeze response
neurons.text: What: Paralysis when neither fighting nor fleeing seems possible; the voice cuts out, the mind goes blank.

neurons.title: Fawn response
neurons.text: What: Appeasing the threat by pleasing the aggressor and suppressing one's own needs. Often seen in people who grew up with angry or unpredictable parents.

neurons.title: Trauma triggers
neurons.text: What: A smell, sound, word or situation that recalls a painful past event sends the person back into that moment's emotional and bodily state. The reaction is out of proportion to the present event.

neurons.title: Burnout
neurons.text: What: Emotional exhaustion, detachment and a sense of meaninglessness at the end of prolonged stress.

neurons.title: Learned helplessness
neurons.text:
What: After repeated exposure to uncontrollable bad events, giving up even when control becomes possible.
Source: Seligman.

neurons.title: Psychological trauma
neurons.text:
What: An event that overwhelms the mind's capacity to cope: violence, assault, sudden death of someone loved, betrayal by someone trusted, helplessness in the face of danger. The memory is stored differently: as raw fragments of sensation and emotion rather than a story, so it keeps intruding into the present. Trauma changes how safe the world feels, how much others can be trusted and how the person sees themselves. It does not fade at the normal speed of forgetting; it lingers for months or years and resurfaces when triggered.
Source: Herman (Trauma and Recovery); van der Kolk; Brewin (dual representation); DSM-5 acute stress and PTSD criteria.

neurons.title: Acute stress reaction
neurons.text: What: The first minutes to days after a traumatic event. Not calm processing: shock, disbelief ("this isn't happening"), shaking, racing heart, nausea, ragged breath, ringing ears, tunnel vision. Speech breaks into fragments or stops; the person may stare, go silent, repeat one word, laugh wrongly, or act on autopilot. Time feels slowed or missing. Clear, composed sentences about what happened are rare in this phase; the full emotion often arrives later.

neurons.title: Emotional numbing
neurons.text: What: The mind turns emotion down to survive: flat voice, blank face, feeling nothing where pain should be, unable to cry, detached from people who were close. Others may mistake it for calm or coldness. It can switch suddenly into flooding (sobbing, rage) when something cracks it.

neurons.title: Intrusive memories
neurons.text: What: Unwanted fragments of the event (an image, a sound, a smell, a word) break into the mind without warning, often in the present tense, as if it is happening again. The body reacts as it did then. The person loses the thread of conversation, goes pale, startles, or stops mid-sentence.

links.why: when the mind circles it on purpose

neurons.title: Hypervigilance
keys: sit with my back to the wall
neurons.text: What: After danger, the body refuses to stand down: scanning rooms, startling at sudden sounds or touch, flinching when someone moves fast, needing exits in view, irritability, poor sleep. Touch from the person or situation linked to the trauma can feel like a threat.

neurons.title: Survivor's guilt
neurons.text: What: Surviving when someone else did not feels like a debt or a crime: "it should have been me", "I was right there", replaying what could have been done differently. It can turn into self-punishment, recklessness, or refusing to be happy.

links.why: when the lost one was loved

neurons.title: Self-blame after trauma
neurons.text: What: Blaming oneself is the mind's attempt to regain control ("if it was my fault, I could have prevented it, so the world is still predictable"). After assault or betrayal it is especially common and especially unfair. It feeds shame and silence.

neurons.title: Nightmares
neurons.text: What: The event or its emotional core returns at night; the person wakes up sweating, shaking, sometimes fighting the air. Sleep becomes something to avoid, and exhaustion makes everything else worse.

neurons.title: Delayed reaction
neurons.text: What: Someone may function almost normally right after the event, then collapse hours or days later when they are finally safe or alone: sudden sobbing, rage, panic, or physical illness. Being "fine" at first does not mean the event did not matter.

neurons.title: Traumatic grief
neurons.text: What: Grief made heavier by how the death happened: sudden, violent, or witnessed. Normal grief (denial, anger, bargaining, sadness) is mixed with trauma: the death scene replays, the person cannot remember the loved one without remembering the end. Anniversaries, places and objects carry it. It does not resolve in days; it can define months.

neurons.title: Shattered trust
neurons.text: What: When the harm came from a person, the bond with that person is broken: fear or revulsion in their presence, flinching at their touch, anger that can be cold or explosive, inability to be alone with them. Trust in people like them, and in one's own judgement, is damaged too. Rebuilding takes a long time and is never guaranteed.

neurons.title: Values
neurons.text:
What: Lasting goals about what matters in life; they act as a compass in choices. Schwartz defines ten universal values and arranges them in a circle: neighboring values are compatible, opposite ones conflict (self-direction ↔ conformity/tradition; power ↔ benevolence).
Source: Shalom Schwartz.

neurons.title: Self-direction
neurons.text: What: Thinking independently, choosing one's own path, creating, exploring.

neurons.title: Stimulation value
neurons.text: What: A life full of excitement, novelty and challenge.

neurons.title: Hedonism
neurons.text: What: Pleasure and sensory gratification.

neurons.title: Achievement
neurons.text: What: Personal success through demonstrating competence by social standards.

neurons.title: Security value
neurons.text: What: Safety, stability and harmony of oneself, one's family and society.

neurons.title: Tradition
neurons.text: What: Respect for and commitment to cultural or religious traditions.

neurons.title: Benevolence
neurons.text: What: Caring for and enhancing the welfare of the people close to oneself.

neurons.title: Universalism
neurons.text: What: Understanding, appreciating and protecting the welfare of all people and nature.

neurons.title: Morality
neurons.text:
What: Most moral judgments are made through fast intuitions, not reasoning; reason finds justifications afterwards. According to Haidt there are six moral foundations, and people weight them differently; political and cultural conflicts are rooted here.
Source: Jonathan Haidt, Moral Foundations Theory.

neurons.title: Care foundation
neurons.text: What: Not causing harm, protecting the vulnerable, mercy.

neurons.title: Fairness foundation
neurons.text: What: Justice, reciprocity, not cheating; giving people what they deserve and punishing cheaters.

neurons.title: Loyalty foundation
neurons.text: What: Loyalty to group, family, partner and friends; treating betrayal as the gravest offense.

neurons.title: Authority
neurons.text: What: Respect for legitimate hierarchy, tradition and rules.

neurons.title: Sanctity foundation
neurons.text: What: Bodily and spiritual purity, sacredness, avoiding behaviors seen as disgusting.

neurons.title: Liberty foundation
neurons.text: What: Opposing domination and bullying; nobody should crush anybody.
